serp_review.query: can i clean gmail without giving a tool oauth access
serp_review.observation: One standard web search returned a Show HN / Indie Hackers / AlternativeTo trio for one product ('Clear Mail for Gmail') claiming local, no-OAuth processing, a local-first Gmail API tool needing user-supplied OAuth credentials, and forum threads (Vivaldi, Firetrust, a GitLab issue) on IMAP/password login that predate Google's removal of password sign-in. No result compared the routes, explained that DOM site access is still broad access, or pointed out where each route is (not) listed for revocation.
serp_review.limitation: One standard US web search; result pages were not opened individually; not a Google ranking capture.

information_gain: A route-by-route table of ways to clean Gmail without an OAuth consent (native Gmail, page-based Chrome extension, IMAP client with app password, own Apps Script) showing what is granted, what it can reach, whether it appears on Google's third-party connections page, and how to stop it. It also corrects two misconceptions in the sampled results: the forum advice that IMAP with a password avoids OAuth (Gmail no longer supports password sign-in; app passwords are Google-discouraged and unscoped), and the implication that 'no OAuth' extensions see less (content scripts with mail.google.com access read and change Gmail pages and are revoked in Chrome, not Google Account).
overlap_check: Pending sibling draft is-it-safe-to-use-gmail-cleanup-extensions (internal/blog-drafts, unpublished) compares OAuth vs extension site access vs native Gmail and has an FAQ on extensions reading mail without Google sign-in. This draft overlaps on that point but its distinct job is the no-OAuth route choice: app passwords/IMAP, Apps Script, revocation location per route, and a native-only procedure. A reviewer should decide whether to cross-link the two and trim the safety draft's no-sign-in FAQ, or merge. Published inbox-cleaner-setup-permissions-recovery is product-specific and is linked rather than repeated.
limitations: Source and documentation review only. No third-party tool, mail client or app password was set up or tested, no live mailbox test was run, and no screenshots exist.
Google and Chrome pages were read through a summarising fetch tool, not saved verbatim; quotations and UI labels (On select, Delete it) should be rechecked.

The Chrome Web Store listing describes an OAuth (identity, gmail.readonly, gmail.modify) build while repository manifest 3.3.1 does not; the uploaded package was not inspected. This blocks publication until resolved.
Inbox Cleaner statements come from repository source and product-facts reviewed for 3.2.1, not from the installed store package or a network capture.
The extension row assumes a page-based extension without its own network or token logic; individual extensions can differ, which the article states.
Workspace admin controls over app passwords, third-party apps and extensions are out of scope beyond noting some work/school accounts lack app passwords.
SERP review was one standard search sample.
